candidates.name: Half-Kneeling Landmine Press

distinctFrom.why: kneeling stance removes leg drive and back-leg anti-rotation contribution entirely, unlike the standing single-arm version; also distinct from the existing "Landmine Press (Abs)" row, whose name-derived position is standing, not kneeling

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Kneeling limb opposite the pressing arm by convention; a common shoulder-stability accessory.

candidates.name: Rotational Landmine Press

distinctFrom.why: the trunk actively rotates into the press (hip and torso turn drives the bar), rather than pressing from a fixed square stance; a rotational-power emphasis the stationary press does not have

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Distinct from the existing "Landmine Press (Abs)" row too: that row is a stationary anti-rotation press (resisting rotation); this one deliberately produces rotation as part of the rep.

candidates.name: Landmine Meadows Row

distinctFrom.why: a bent-over, slightly turned stance (torso angled toward the bar end) with a shorter, more lat-stretched ROM than the square-stance single-arm row it is often confused with

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Named after John Meadows; distinct hip/torso angle from the standard single-arm landmine row is the coached difference.

candidates.name: Landmine Chest-Supported Row

distinctFrom.why: chest braced against an inclined bench over the bar removes all lower-back and hip involvement, unlike the bent-over two-arm row

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Needs a bench positioned over the landmine sleeve; setup complexity keeps it niche rather than specialist.

candidates.name: Landmine Hack Squat

distinctFrom.why: the bar travels behind/between the calves (hack-squat bar path) rather than held at the chest, shifting the load line behind the body and biasing the quads more directly

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: A hinge-forward torso with the bar close to the heels is the coaching point that separates it from the chest-held Landmine Squat.

candidates.name: Landmine Zercher Squat

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (landmine sleeve vs free barbell); the fixed pivot at the sleeve changes the bar path to an arc rather than a straight vertical line

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Held in the crook of the elbows like the barbell Zercher squat, but anchored at one end.

candidates.name: Landmine Sumo Squat

distinctFrom.why: wide stance with the bar held vertically between the legs, shifting the load line and emphasis toward adductors/glutes versus the narrow-stance chest-held squat

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Bar held two-handed at the sleeve end, vertical, between a wide stance; a common landmine goblet-squat substitute.

candidates.name: Landmine Reverse Lunge

distinctFrom.why: new movement family for this corpus: no existing landmine lunge row is seeded

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Bar racked at the chest (as in Landmine Squat) with a reverse step; the arc of the bar assists balance versus a free-weight reverse lunge.

candidates.name: Landmine Anti-Rotation Press (Half-Kneeling)

distinctFrom.why: the trunk actively RESISTS rotation while the arms press out and back in (an isometric-in-motion anti-rotation demand), the opposite intent of Landmine Rotation and Landmine Twist, which deliberately produce trunk rotation

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Kneeling, both arms extend the bar out from the chest and return without letting the hips or shoulders turn toward the anchor; also distinguished from "Landmine Press (Abs)" (existing row, standing per its name-derived position) by the explicit kneeling stance and anti-rotation coaching cue.

candidates.name: Landmine Shrug

distinctFrom.why: new movement family for this corpus: no existing landmine shrug row is seeded

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Bar held at the hips (as for a landmine RDL) and shrugged; a rare substitute when no dumbbells/trap bar are free.

candidates.name: Landmine Floor Press

distinctFrom.why: lying on the floor removes leg drive and shortens the ROM at the bottom, the same floor-vs-standing distinction the corpus already draws between "Close-Grip Bench Press" and "Close-Grip Floor Press"

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Rare setup (needs the sleeve height to clear a lying lifter) but attested as a shoulder-friendly landmine pressing option.

candidates.name: Landmine Thruster

distinctFrom.why: the squat continues into a press at the top of every rep (single-arm, bar angles up and away from the shoulder) rather than stopping at standing

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Not classified ballistic under EL-7; a continuous squat-to-press, not a launch.

candidates.name: Landmine Split Squat

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (landmine vs barbell); the bar is racked at the chest and its arc assists balance, rather than a bar on the back or held free

sources: Established S&C coaching literature (landmine training texts/courses: e.g. Perform Better, EliteFTS landmine programming guides)
candidates.notes: Rear foot may be elevated (Bulgarian-style) or flat; same distinguishing mechanism either way, so kept as one row.

rejected.name: Landmine Push Press
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 (leg-drive assistance on a single-arm landmine press is a coaching cue on the existing "Landmine Chest Press (Single-Arm)" and "Half-Kneeling Landmine Press" rows, not a separately attested named movement in the corpus’s naming convention)

rejected.name: Landmine Clean
rejected.reason: unattested as a standard named landmine movement distinct from a deadlift-to-shoulder shrug; not a recognised drill in the checked sources

rejected.name: Landmine Woodchopper
rejected.reason: duplicate of 'Landmine Rotation'/'Landmine Twist' (same standing rotational core pattern already seeded twice)

observations: Landmine Rotation and Landmine Twist are already both seeded (back, abs, isolation, rotation subregion) and read as the same movement under two names; flagged here as an existing-corpus duplicate for the lead, not something this agent renames or removes.

"Landmine Press (Abs)" already exists (abs primary, movementPattern core) and is mechanically close to a half-kneeling or standing anti-rotation press; its name does not say "kneeling" and its name-derived position is standing, so this agent treated the new Half-Kneeling Landmine Press / Rotational Landmine Press / Landmine Anti-Rotation Press candidates as distinct by stance and by producing-vs-resisting rotation, and recorded the reasoning in each candidate rather than guessing which the existing row already is.
